RheaRouter Vision Model Benchmark

Comprehensive Analysis of Local Vision LLMs for Production Deployment

📅 November 25, 2025 🖥️ NVIDIA RTX A2000 8GB 🧪 7 Test Suites 📊 500+ Inference Requests

Abstract

This benchmark evaluates four open-source vision language models—Qwen2.5-VL 7B, MiniCPM-V 8B, LLaVA 7B, and Gemma3n—for production OCR and document processing tasks running on commodity hardware (NVIDIA RTX A2000 8GB). Through 500+ inference tests across seven comprehensive test suites, we systematically measured OCR accuracy under adversarial conditions including rotation, blur, noise, lighting variations, and JPEG compression artifacts.

Our findings reveal Qwen2.5-VL 7B as the clear leader for document processing, achieving 95% average OCR accuracy compared to 79% for MiniCPM-V, 32% for LLaVA, and 5% for Gemma3n. Critically, Qwen maintained perfect 100% accuracy on serial number recognition across 11 of 16 degradation scenarios—a capability essential for inventory management, asset tracking, and compliance documentation.

This report demonstrates that self-hosted vision inference is now viable for enterprise deployments, offering significant cost savings over cloud API services while maintaining full data sovereignty. Organizations processing 100,000+ documents annually can expect ROI within weeks when migrating from cloud vision APIs to self-hosted solutions like RheaRouter.

TEST 7 OCR Stress Test: Adversarial Text Recognition

This test generates images with known text, applies systematic degradations (rotation, blur, noise, lighting changes), and measures how accurately each model can recover the original text.

Overall model performance across 320 adversarial OCR tests (5 text types × 16 degradations × 4 models)

Model Average Score Best Degradation Status
Qwen2.5-VL 7B 95% Light Noise (97%) Production Ready
MiniCPM-V 8B 79% Baseline/Dark (90%) Production Ready
LLaVA 7B 32% Blur Light (43%) Limited Use
Gemma3n 5% All (5%) Not Recommended

Performance by Degradation Type

Understanding how models handle specific image quality issues helps determine which preprocessing steps are needed for production deployment.

Comparison of top 3 models across 10 common image degradation scenarios

💡 Key Insight: Robustness Matters

Qwen2.5-VL maintains >90% accuracy even with heavy blur (93%) and rotation up to 30° (91%). This robustness means less preprocessing required in production, saving both compute time and complexity.

Serial Number OCR: The Ultimate Precision Test

Serial numbers, UUIDs, and MAC addresses require perfect character-by-character accuracy. This is the hardest test for vision models because a single character error makes the entire result useless.

Qwen2.5-VL achieved 100% accuracy on 11 out of 16 degradation scenarios for serial number recognition

📋 Production Recommendation

For applications requiring serial number, barcode, or precise alphanumeric extraction, Qwen2.5-VL 7B is the only viable choice. MiniCPM-V struggles with blur (17%) and noise (45%), while LLaVA is essentially unusable for this task (8% baseline).

models:

    name: qwen2.5vl:7b

    preprocess:

  fallback:

    name: llava:7b

server:
  max_concurrent_requests: 3
  request_timeout: 60
  model_swap_cooldown: 5s

Cost Savings vs OpenRouter

Self-hosting vision models provides dramatic cost savings compared to cloud API services, especially at scale. The following analysis compares the total annual cost of using OpenRouter's vision API (~$0.015/image) versus running RheaRouter on dedicated hardware.

💰 Break-Even Analysis

Break-even point: ~17,500 documents/year (~48 documents/day)

Organizations processing more than 50 documents per day will see positive ROI within the first year. At enterprise scale (1M+ docs/year), self-hosting saves $14,637 annually—a 97% cost reduction.

📊 Cost Assumptions

  • OpenRouter: $0.015/image average (GPT-4V, Claude vision pricing)
  • Hardware: RTX A2000 $450 amortized over 3 years = $150/year
  • Power: 60W × 24h × 365 days × $0.12/kWh = $63/year
  • Maintenance: $50/year (estimated labor/updates)
  • Per-inference cost: $0.0001 (marginal electricity)
